2027 is officially bringing FOUR major releases to Netflix, with THE ONE PIECE, BRIDGERTON, NARNIA, and SCOOBY-DOO all preparing to make next year one of the platform's biggest for beloved franchises.

Greta Gerwig's NARNIA: THE MAGICIAN'S NEPHEW will arrive in theaters on February 12 before streaming on Netflix on April 2, exploring the magical origins of Narnia with a cast that includes Meryl Streep, Daniel Craig, and Emma Mackey.

SCOOBY-DOO: ORIGINS is also officially arriving in 2027, introducing a live-action version of Mystery Inc. with Mckenna Grace as Daphne Blake. The series will explore how the legendary mystery-solving gang first came together, including a real Great Dane portraying Scooby-Doo.

DC Studios' new boss Jeremy Latcham previously worked at Marvel, where his "guiding light" was to make superhero movies for everyone.

“In the old Marvel days, there’s this great story about my Meemaw and Peepaw because they became, like, a joke in the editing room – that we were making the movie for my grandparents in Oklahoma,” Latcham previously said in a separate interview with GamesRadar+. “If they weren’t gonna understand it, [it was] never going to work for  anybody… I think that’s kind of the fun of these movies, of adapting  material – finding a way to make it for everybody. 🦷 Scientists Develop Special Gel That Could Help Repair Tooth Enamel in Just 14 Days

Researchers at the University of Nottingham in England have developed a promising new approach to repairing damaged tooth enamel using a specially engineered bio-inspired gel.

The pioneering research, led by Professor Alvaro Mata and Dr. Abshar Hasan, was published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Communications.

The team developed a synthetic gel designed to work alongside the body's natural chemistry, potentially opening a new direction for regenerative dentistry.

Unlike bones, teeth cannot naturally regrow enamel once it has been lost. This is because the cells responsible for producing enamel die before teeth fully emerge, leaving the body unable to replace damaged enamel on its own.

To address this limitation, researchers engineered an organic material using specially designed proteins known as elastin-like recombinamers (ELRs).

When applied to a damaged tooth, the gel creates an extremely thin, microscopic framework that acts as a scaffold for mineral regeneration.

It attracts calcium and phosphate ions naturally present in human saliva and organizes them into structured mineral crystals that resemble the natural composition and architecture of tooth enamel.

According to the research description, this process can produce an organized mineral layer within just 14 days, potentially restoring important properties such as hardness and structural strength.

🔬 A Potential Breakthrough for Regenerative Dentistry
The technology could offer a new way to address enamel damage without relying entirely on conventional restorative treatments.

By encouraging minerals naturally available in saliva to form an enamel-like structure, the approach could potentially help repair early tooth damage and protect weakened teeth.

If further research and clinical testing confirm its effectiveness and safety, the technology could eventually contribute to new treatments for tooth sensitivity, enamel erosion and other forms of dental damage.

However, the research should not be interpreted as proof that people can currently regrow fully lost tooth enamel at home. Further development and clinical validation will be needed before such treatments become widely available.

Nepal Police Deploys 107 Dogs Across 13 Locations, Leo Takes Top Honor This Year

A specially trained police dog named Leo has been awarded the title of 'Best Police Dog of the Year' by Nepal Police in recognition of its important contribution to search and rescue operations during the Bhote Koshi River flood.

According to the Nepal Police Canine Office, Leo played a significant role in searching for people who went missing after a devastating flood struck the Bhote Koshi River on Bhadra 10.

The dog was honored on the occasion of Kukur Tihar, a festival dedicated to celebrating and worshipping dogs in Nepal.

Leo's recognition highlights the important role trained police dogs play in emergency response operations, particularly during natural disasters when locating missing people can be extremely challenging.

Nepal Police regularly deploys specially trained dogs to identify weapons, explosives and narcotics, as well as to assist in search and rescue operations during natural disasters.

According to the Canine Office, Nepal Police currently operates 107 dogs of different breeds across 13 locations nationwide. These dogs are actively involved in criminal investigations and various specialized operations.

Leo's achievement has added another special moment to this year's Kukur Tihar celebrations, recognizing the dedication and contribution of a four-legged member of Nepal's rescue and security teams.

Nepal Deports 86 Bangladeshis in 10 Months as Crackdown on Illegal Foreigners Intensifies
Nepal has deported 86 Bangladeshi nationals over the past 10 months for alleged immigration violations, illegal employment and suspected involvement in criminal activities, according to government statistics.

Bangladeshi citizens are now the second-largest group of foreign nationals deported from Nepal after Chinese citizens.

According to BBC Nepali, 51 Bangladeshi nationals were deported in the four-month period from Shrawan to Ashoj alone. Meanwhile, 18 Bangladeshi citizens are currently being held at the Department of Immigration.

In the latest incident, four Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian citizen were arrested from different locations in Kathmandu on Kartik 16. They were subsequently handed over to the Department of Immigration for further investigation.

Police officials say some foreign nationals have been found entering Nepal on tourist visas but engaging in unauthorized employment. Others reportedly continue staying in the country even after their visas expire or enter through illegal routes.

Authorities are also investigating suspected involvement in criminal activities, including online fraud.

According to police data, a total of 117,682 Bangladeshi nationals travelled to and from Nepal by air over the past year. Of them, 58,879 entered Nepal, while 58,803 departed from the country.

The Department of Immigration says foreign nationals found violating visa conditions are required to pay applicable fees and fines before deportation. In some cases, they are also barred from entering Nepal for several years.

However, officials have clarified that individuals found to have committed criminal offences will face further legal action under the relevant laws.

Authorities are continuing to monitor foreign nationals suspected of violating immigration regulations and engaging in unlawful activities.

For nine months, researchers searched the waters around Ecuador's Galápagos Islands hoping to find blue whales. But not a single whale was spotted during their expedition.

Between October 2025 and July 2026, scientists surveyed areas where these ocean giants had historically been seen. Their search coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions linked to El Niño.

Researchers suspect the warmer water may have disrupted the availability of krill, the blue whales' main food source, causing them to move toward cooler, more productive waters farther south.

Scientists emphasize that the whales may have migrated elsewhere rather than died. Their disappearance from the Galápagos highlights how changing ocean conditions can affect the movements of even the largest animals on Earth.

Researchers hope the blue whales will return when ocean temperatures and feeding conditions improve.

Source: Live Science, November 2, 2026.

The real story: A rule published in Mexico's official gazette on October 14, 2026, and in force from October 15, cut the area where gillnets are banned in the Upper Gulf of California from 11,106 to 1,562 square kilometers, an 86% reduction. The government says it follows scientific recommendations and supports fishing communities. Conservation groups say it could accelerate extinction of the vaquita, with only about 7 to 10 left. Source: La Razón de México, published October 15, 2026, with Reuters and Center for Biological Diversity statements.

The vaquita is the world's smallest and rarest porpoise, found only in Mexico's Upper Gulf of California, and gillnets are the main reason its numbers collapsed. On October 14, 2026, Mexico published a rule that sharply changed the map. The area where gillnets are banned shrank from 11,106 to 1,562 square kilometers, an 86 percent cut that took effect on October 15 and reopens roughly 9,500 square kilometers to that kind of fishing.

The government's case: Semarnat, the environment ministry, said the new rule focuses protection on the places where vaquitas have most often been recorded, following recommendations from the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita. It keeps the Zero Tolerance Zone and adds surveillance measures. President Claudia Sheinbaum and Baja California governor Marina del Pilar Ávila said it supports fishing communities such as San Felipe, Golfo de Santa Clara and Puerto Peñasco. Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a leading vaquita scientist who took part in the committee, told Reuters he hoped a smaller area could concentrate efforts to save the animal.

The critics' case: the Center for Biological Diversity said Mexico's rules will "accelerate the vaquita's extinction," arguing that the new rule protects the porpoise in only a fraction of its historical range. The numbers behind the argument are small: the 2025 monitoring saw between seven and ten vaquitas, and the conservation agency Conanp reported three sightings in May 2026 outside the Zero Tolerance Zone. It is a decision that two sides describe in opposite ways, and the animal at the center of it numbers fewer than a dozen.

An extraordinary encounter off Newport Beach, California, has brought a rare group of marine mammals back into the spotlight.

On November 3, 2026, whale-watching crews spotted approximately 70 short-finned pilot whales just five miles offshore. According to local whale-watching operators, it was the first documented sighting of the species in the area since 2015.

Despite their name, pilot whales are actually members of the dolphin family. They are highly social animals that travel in close-knit groups and dive deep into the ocean to hunt squid.

Researchers and whale-watching operators believe changing ocean conditions associated with El Niño may have influenced their appearance, although the exact reason remains unknown.

For local whale watchers, seeing such a large group after more than a decade was an unforgettable experience.

Source: Newport Signal, November 5, 2026; NOAA Fisheries.

An unexpected discovery has brought new hope to scientists studying one of the world's most endangered whale species.

Researchers photographed an unidentified North Atlantic right whale calf swimming beside its 38-year-old mother, known as Silt, near Anticosti Island, Quebec, in September 2026. After analyzing the photographs and research records, scientists confirmed that the young whale had not previously been counted.

The discovery brings the total number of calves identified during the 2026 birthing season to 24, making it the most successful season since 2009.

However, only around 380 North Atlantic right whales remain, including approximately 70 reproductive-age females. Ship strikes and entanglement in fishing gear continue to threaten their survival.

For researchers, finding another healthy calf is a welcome reason for hope.

Source: Associated Press, November 6, 2026.

A scientific investigation has revealed that a male orca found dead in Scotland may have been much older than researchers originally expected.

The whale stranded on the island of South Uist in 2015. Scientists later examined his teeth using radiocarbon dating, a technique that measures traces of radioactive carbon left by nuclear weapons testing during the mid-20th century.

The results suggested that the male may have been around 65 years old or older, potentially making him one of the oldest male orcas ever recorded.

Researchers from several Scottish institutions participated in the investigation, using the chemical record preserved in the whale’s teeth to estimate his age.

The discovery shows how even the remains of a whale can reveal important information about the lives and longevity of these remarkable ocean predators.

Source: Whale and Dolphin Conservation, November 6, 2026.

An unusual tracking project is revealing the remarkable movements of two killer whales traveling along South Africa’s coastline.

In October 2026, researchers from Sea Search fitted a satellite tag to a female orca known as part of a pair nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde. The tag began transmitting their movements from False Bay near Simon’s Town.

Their recorded journey took them north past Table Bay, Saldanha Bay, and Lamberts Bay toward the Northern Cape. At one point, the pair covered approximately 100 kilometers in a single day.

Researchers described their highly coastal travel pattern as unusual for killer whales in South Africa. By combining satellite tracking, photographs, and biological samples, scientists hope to learn more about their movements, diet, habitat use, and interactions with human activities.

The tracking project offers a rare opportunity to follow the journey of wild orcas across an extensive stretch of the South African coast.

Source: Cape Town Etc, November 6, 2026; Sea Search.

“UNDER ACTIVE SNIPER FIRE: HE DRAGGED HIS WOUNDED BROTHER THROUGH THE MUD TO SAFETY.”

On October 31, 2006, in the war-torn city of Karmah near Fallujah in Anbar Province, Iraq, a foot patrol from the 4th Mobile Assault Platoon (Weapons Company, 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines) was moving down a flooded, unpaved alleyway when a single gunshot broke the silence.

An insurgent sniper round struck 22-year-old Lance Corporal Juan Valdez-Castillo in the right arm, entered his chest, collapsed both lungs, ricocheted off a rib, and exited through his back, fracturing a vertebra.

Valdez-Castillo slammed into a cinderblock wall and collapsed into the freezing mud and standing water, suffocating and unable to move.

His squad leader, Sergeant Jesse E. Leach, didn't hesitate:

Sprinting into the Kill Zone: With the sniper still zeroed in on the alley, Sgt. Leach stepped directly into the open line of fire without waiting for suppressive coverage.

The Mud Drag: Grabbing the drag handle of Valdez-Castillo’s body armor with his left hand while keeping his M4 rifle aimed downrange with his right, Leach hauled his 200-pound teammate backward through thick, viscous canal mud toward the shelter of a concrete wall.

Capturing History: Embedded New York Times photojournalist Joao Silva and reporter C.J. Chivers captured the raw, straining rescue in real time, producing one of the most defining photographs of brotherhood in modern combat history.

Refusing to Quit: Behind cover, Leach applied emergency chest seals and stanched the catastrophic bleeding, stabilizing Valdez-Castillo until medevac forces arrived.

Sergeant Jesse Leach was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with Combat "V" for his valor under fire.

Against all odds, Juan Valdez-Castillo survived. After extensive surgeries and rehabilitation, he returned to Iraq, deployed to Afghanistan, retired as a sergeant, and later graduated from law school to spend his life advocating for wounded veterans.

“No Marine left behind is not a motto. It is an unbreakable promise written in blood and mud.”

“MY HELICOPTER CRASHED INTO BIN LADEN’S COMPOUND. AFTER EXTORTION 17, I WANTED TO DIE.” — SEAL Team 6 Operator Alex West on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most raw, heartbreaking conversations on The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #114), former DEVGRU operator Alex West opened up about survivor’s guilt, post-traumatic stress, and the invisible scars of war.

After enlisting at 17 and becoming the youngest operator ever selected for SEAL Team 6, West survived 15 combat deployments—including the stealth Black Hawk crash during Operation Neptune Spear—only to lose his closest brothers three months later when callsign Extortion 17 was shot down in the Tangi Valley.

In his own words:

“I was in the tail of the helicopter when our bird lost lift and slammed into the courtyard wall inside Osama bin Laden’s compound in Abbottabad. The tail snapped, rotors chewed into the dirt, and we scrambled out directly into the assault.

We pulled off the biggest raid in modern history. But just three months later, Extortion 17 was shot down.

In a single second, 30 American service members—my entire squadron, the guys who stood next to me in Abbottabad, my mentors, my best friends—were completely incinerated in the Tangi Valley.

When that happened, my soul broke.

I went home and spiraled into pure darkness. I was drinking myself to death every single night just to make the screaming in my head stop. I would sit on the edge of my bed with a loaded pistol in my hand, staring at the floor, crying, begging for the courage to pull the trigger.

Surviving the raid that took out the world's most wanted terrorist meant nothing when all the men you loved were in body bags.”

Surviving the most dangerous missions on earth only to face your hardest battle alone in a dark room at home is a reality thousands of combat veterans know all too well.

Long before he stood in the dust and smoke of Lower Manhattan, Rick Rescorla was already a legend of American military history — the young platoon leader pictured on the cover of We Were Soldiers Once… and Young who rallied his men through the savage 1965 Battle of Ia Drang.

Decades later, as head of corporate security for Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center, Rescorla brought that same battle-tested discipline to civilian life. Following the 1993 truck bombing, he concluded that the towers remained vulnerable to an aerial attack and instituted mandatory, unannounced evacuation drills every few months. Executives grumbled about lost trading hours, but Rescorla was unyielding. He timed workers with a stopwatch, training thousands of employees to navigate dark stairwells until moving in an emergency became muscle memory.

On the morning of September 11, 2001, when American Airlines Flight 11 struck Tower One, building announcements blared over the PA system instructing workers in Tower Two to remain at their desks. Rescorla refused. Shouting into his bullhorn that everything above the impact zone was burning and that their building was in danger, he immediately ordered the complete evacuation of Morgan Stanley’s 22 floors.

As thousands of anxious workers descended the crowded stairwells, Rescorla walked beside them with his megaphone, singing Cornish marching songs and Welsh battle hymns to banish panic. Between choruses, he smiled and told his people to remain calm, proud, and steady. Over 2,600 Morgan Stanley employees made it out alive that morning.

After clearing his floors, Rescorla called his best friend Dan Hill from his mobile phone, stating calmly that the dumb bastards were telling him not to evacuate, but that he was getting his people out. When last seen alive on the tenth floor heading back up into the burning tower, colleagues urged him to leave. Rescorla shook his head and replied that as soon as he made sure everyone else was out, he would follow.

Moments later, Tower Two collapsed.

How does true leadership look when routine gives way to crisis?

Fourteen years ago today, on November 9, 2012, Capt. James D. Nehl was killed in action in Gelan, Ghazni Province, Afghanistan. When his dismounted patrol came under enemy fire and his radio operator was shot in the chest, Nehl left his covered position to get to him. He was hit while moving. Wounded, he still managed to call for help over the radio and drag his soldier to safety before he succumbed to his wounds. He was 37 years old.

Nehl's roots ran deep in the Regiment. He spent much of his 18 years as an infantryman with 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment, starting as an enlisted Ranger in Alpha Company before earning his commission. At the time of his death, he was serving with 2nd Battalion, 16th Infantry Regiment, 4th Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division, out of Fort Riley.

He was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal. For years, the men who knew him have argued that saving his radio operator under fire was a valorous act that deserved recognition for valor. Today, at 2nd Ranger Battalion, his wife, mother, and son received his upgraded award.

It took 14 years, but the record now reflects what his Ranger brothers knew all along. RLTW.

First flown in 1974, the F-16 Fighting Falcon is still being built today, more than 50 years later.

With about 4,600 produced, the jet pilots nicknamed the "Viper" is the most-produced fourth-generation fighter in the world. Only far older designs, like the Soviet MiG-21, were ever built in larger numbers.

It was revolutionary from the start: the first production fighter deliberately built slightly unstable for agility, controlled by a computerized fly-by-wire system, with a frameless bubble canopy, a reclined seat, a sidestick, and the ability to pull 9 g's.

That blend of performance, affordability, and versatility made it one of America's greatest export successes, flown today by around 25 nations. And it's not done: brand-new Block 70 Vipers are rolling off the line in Greenville, South Carolina, right now.

More than 2,000 F-16s still fly worldwide, and the type is expected to serve into the 2040s, a Cold War design that simply refuses to quit.

An insurgent sniper round struck 22-year-old Lance Corporal Juan Valdez-Castillo in the right arm, entered his chest, collapsed both lungs, ricocheted off a rib, and exited through his back, fracturing a vertebra.

Valdez-Castillo slammed into a cinderblock wall and collapsed into the freezing mud and standing water, suffocating and unable to move.

His squad leader, Sergeant Jesse E. Leach, didn't hesitate:

Sprinting into the Kill Zone: With the sniper still zeroed in on the alley, Sgt. Leach stepped directly into the open line of fire without waiting for suppressive coverage.

The Mud Drag: Grabbing the drag handle of Valdez-Castillo’s body armor with his left hand while keeping his M4 rifle aimed downrange with his right, Leach hauled his 200-pound teammate backward through thick, viscous canal mud toward the shelter of a concrete wall.

Capturing History: Embedded New York Times photojournalist Joao Silva and reporter C.J. Chivers captured the raw, straining rescue in real time, producing one of the most defining photographs of brotherhood in modern combat history.

Sergeant Jesse Leach was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with Combat "V" for his valor under fire.

Against all odds, Juan Valdez-Castillo survived. After extensive surgeries and rehabilitation, he returned to Iraq, deployed to Afghanistan, retired as a sergeant, and later graduated from law school to spend his life advocating for wounded veterans.

“No Marine left behind is not a motto. It is an unbreakable promise written in blood and mud.”

Surviving the most dangerous missions on earth only to face your hardest battle alone in a dark room at home is a reality thousands of combat veterans know all too well.

Valdez-Castillo slammed into a cinderblock wall and collapsed into the freezing mud and standing water, suffocating and unable to move.

Sprinting into the Kill Zone: With the sniper still zeroed in on the alley, Sgt. Leach stepped directly into the open line of fire without waiting for suppressive coverage.

The Mud Drag: Grabbing the drag handle of Valdez-Castillo’s body armor with his left hand while keeping his M4 rifle aimed downrange with his right, Leach hauled his 200-pound teammate backward through thick, viscous canal mud toward the shelter of a concrete wall.

Capturing History: Embedded New York Times photojournalist Joao Silva and reporter C.J. Chivers captured the raw, straining rescue in real time, producing one of the most defining photographs of brotherhood in modern combat history.

Refusing to Quit: Behind cover, Leach applied emergency chest seals and stanched the catastrophic bleeding, stabilizing Valdez-Castillo until medevac forces arrived.

Sergeant Jesse Leach was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with Combat "V" for his valor under fire.

Trainees practice rapid runway crater repair, expeditionary refueling operations, weapons loading, aircraft marshaling, casualty evacuation, and forward perimeter defense against simulated ground assaults. The program even incorporates analog map-and-compass navigation drills to ensure future airmen can coordinate operations across a chaotic flightline when GPS signals and digital communications are jammed or destroyed by an adversary.

When Wilzcek and Pushkin saw Alvarez’s difficulties, they ran into the open to help. But as the three moved back toward cover, two RPGs exploded 10 meters away, knocking them down and sending a volley of shrapnel into Alvarez’s right knee. The men stood up and continued dragging their comrade to the safety of a nearby courtyard.

After establishing a safe area for the injured, Pushkin and Wilzcek ran back and forth several times from the courtyard into the line of fire to rescue trapped soldiers. Meanwhile, the RPG explosions had also injured Row’s elbow with shrapnel. Even so, he continued firing on the enemy position to help the others reach safety. Once everyone was clear, Row, who was alone in the middle of the street, called for help. As Row remembered later, “I was trapped in the street, and [Pushkin and Wilzcek] pulled me out of there.”

The squad was now in the courtyard, and medical assistance was being administered – but their work was not done: enemy fire continued to light up the area. When the squad started planning the next phase, Alvarez refused to be moved with the other injured soldiers, staying to help in the fight.

The insurgents, seeing the evacuation in progress, focused their fire on the rescuers. Wilzcek, already on the roof, began firing back. After clearing the rooms below, Pushkin and his team hurried up to the roof to help Wilzcek. Row grabbed a Bunker Defeat Munition – a shoulder-launched explosive for use against fortified positions – but his injured elbow prevented him from using it. He ran up to the roof, handed the weapon to Pushkin, and helped guide Pushkin toward the targets. With Row and Wilzcek providing cover fire, Pushkin took aim and fired, destroying the enemy’s position and killing a number of insurgents. With that, the squad was able to leave the area safely.

A bullet took nearly nine full seconds in flight before striking its target—shattering the confirmed world record for the longest sniper kill in human history.

At a distance of over 41 football fields, hitting a human-sized target defies conventional ballistic physics:

The Coriolis Effect: Because the bullet stayed airborne for nearly nine seconds, the sniper team had to calculate the physical rotation of the Earth beneath the projectile.

Massive Bullet Drop: The bullet dropped over 300 feet (100+ meters) from apex to impact, requiring the shooter to angle the rifle high into the sky like an artillery piece.

Shifting Winds: Factoring in temperature, barometric air pressure, humidity, and varying crosswinds across two miles of open water and terrain.

The hardware behind the shot was just as extreme: the custom "Horizon's Lord" (Volodar Obriyu) anti-materiel precision rifle, measuring over six feet in length.

In the bottom of the photo, you can see why this rifle reaches where standard weapons fail:

On the right is a standard .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) round.

On the left is the monster 12.7x114mm HL cartridge—a massive 14.5mm anti-aircraft casing necked down to fire a heavy .50-caliber precision match bullet at over 3,400 feet per second, keeping the projectile supersonic far past two miles.

The shot surpassed the previous world record held by a Canadian JTF-2 sniper in Iraq (3,540 meters) and pushed the outer limits of extreme long-range shooting.

 If you are coming into this room with sorrow or to feel sorry for my wounds, go elsewhere. That sign became our line in the sand. You don’t get to mourn me while I’m still standing.”

Jason Redman endured 37 surgeries, extensive facial reconstruction, and years of physical therapy, going on to write The Trident and Overcome and dedicating his life to helping combat veterans conquer their own life ambushes.

Capt. Brian Erickson, a pilot from the 75th Fighter Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor on July 11, 2008.

Capt. Brian Erickson, 75th FS chief of mission planning, earned the medal while deployed to Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, for providing ground alert close air support to a German Provincial Reconstruction Team that was under nighttime fire from insurgents in a valley of the Hindu-Kush mountains.

"I'm extremely impressed with the way Captain Erickson handled himself out there," said Colonel Kenneth Todorov, 23rd Wing commander, "He provided close air support in hazardous conditions, with no forward air controller and led a successful mission with valor."

On Oct. 16, 2006, Captain Erickson and his wingman, who were then part of the 75th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, received a short-notice call to provide aerial support to six German soldiers trapped between two mountain ranges. They were receiving enemy fire in the form of rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and small-arms fire.

Up until the call, previous flights of non-tactical aircraft had been unable to help the stranded PRT due to their location, limited communication capabilities, and lack of moonlight. Without illumination from the moon or another source, the pilots' night vision goggles provided little assistance.

Once he arrived on scene, Captain Erickson determined there was room for only one aircraft above the mountain tops and just below the clouds. He assigned the safe altitude above the clouds to his wingman, who searched for the insurgents' location with his advanced targeting pod and night vision goggles.

As Captain Erickson flew his A-10 deep into the moonless valley, where the only light on the ground was from insurgent weapons fire, his wingman flew above to relay reports about where the weapon bursts were coming from. Before Capt. Erickson could employ any of his own weapons, he needed to determine the exact location of the PRT to avoid friendly fire.

"I initially had my infrared sensor on to pinpoint the location of the insurgents. The problem with using the infrared was that every time a rocket-propelled grenade went off, the glow impeded my ability to navigate the dark canyon. The whole screen would go white, and I couldn't see outside my cockpit. The only solution was to turn the screens off," said Captain Erickson.

After Captain Erickson turned off his infrared sensor, he continued his low-level runs in search of the PRT. This proved an even more difficult task because the PRT's signaling device, an infrared strobe, was malfunctioning, and the German soldiers, who were untrained in communicating with aircraft, continued to take harassing enemy fire. The chaos of the situation was impaired even more by the PRT's limited proficiency in English. These limitations in combination with the enemy fire caused the PRT to provide confusing information on their exact location.

Realizing that time was running out for the PRT, Captain Erickson released a series of covert illumination flares only visible through night vision devices. Able to "see", he used geographic references from the air and ground to narrow down the PRT's location. During this time, the captain and his wingman were able to identify a location where they believed the enemy fire was coming from.

To be sure of the PRT's location, Captain Erickson conducted a low-altitude show-of-force. He flew between the enemy and friendly positions at 2,000 feet and deployed pyrotechnic self-protection flares, which lit the night sky. His hope was that the enemy would alert to his position and break their attack on the PRT long enough for his wingman to search for clues of the enemy's exact position.

"After we located where we thought the insurgents were, I had my wingman light-up the area with his targeting pod," said Captain Erickson. "During this time the weapons-fire against the Germans was also becoming increasingly accurate, and the need to bring the situation to a close was becoming more-and-more imperative. After we were able to determine that we were, in fact, targeting the insurgents and not the pinned-down German PRT team, it was time to take action."

With Captain Erickson's wingman marking the enemy's position with his TGP's infrared pointer, the PRT confirmed the mark as the enemy fire point of origin. In a single pass, Captain Erickson employed 240 30-millimeter rounds from the aircraft's GAU-8 cannon. This completely halted the enemy's fire and saved the lives of six German soldiers.

Captain Erickson and his wingman remained in the area to monitor both the friendly and enemy positions until the Iraqi National Police and International Security Assistance Force Quick Reaction Force were able to reach and recover the PRT and bring them to safety.

Captain Erickson credited the operation's success to his training. Although he was honored to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor for "doing the job he's trained to do," he pointed out a higher honor.

"The real reward was returning those six coalition soldiers safely to the village they were working at as part of the PRT team," said Captain Erickson.

Law enforcement quickly confirmed an active domestic crisis where an armed suspect had taken the lives of his mother and sister before barricading himself inside the residence.

Knowing that innocent lives hung in the balance, SWAT team members moved in to rescue potential survivors and secure the home. As Deputy Parker Perry, a dedicated K9 handler with his partner Brego, and Deputy Mason Acheson, an experienced SWAT sniper and former Washington State Trooper, advanced toward the entrance, the barricaded suspect opened fire without warning.

Both deputies were critically injured in the ambush while shielding their fellow officers. Team members immediately returned fire, safely pulled their wounded brothers from the line of fire, and contained the scene. Deputy Acheson, 35, passed away the following morning. Deputy Perry, 29, remained on life support until his family made the selfless choice to donate his organs, continuing to save lives even after his final watch.

Both men were Washington Army National Guard veterans, devoted husbands, and loving fathers who left behind young children, with Deputy Perry’s wife currently expecting their third baby. Gunnery Sgt. Aubrey McDade
1st Battalion, 8th Marines
Fallujah, Iraq, Nov. 11, 2004
Award: Navy Cross

Shortly after departing their base in Fallujah, then-Sgt. McDade and 1/8 Bravo Company's 1st Platoon entered an alley and encountered an immediate heavy volume of small arms and machine gun fire. In the opening seconds of the engagement, three Marines were seriously wounded as the well positioned and expecting enemy pinned others down. On contact, McDade rushed from the rear of the platoon column toward the kill zone and immediately deployed a machine gun team into the alley to provide suppressive fire on the enemy. After several attempts to reach casualties in the alley were met with heavy, well-aimed machine gun fire, he showed total disregard for his own safety by moving across the alley and successfully extracting the first of three wounded Marines from the kill zone. Aware of the fact that there were still two wounded Marines in the alley, McDade dashed through the heart of the kill zone two more times, each time braving intense enemy fire to successfully retrieve a Marine. After extracting the last casualty from the kill zone, he assisted in their treatment and medical evacuation. His quick thinking and aggressive actions were crucial in saving the lives of two of the three casualties.
